before.exam_tip_html: When an AQA Food Technology question asks you to “explain” something about protein, always link your answer back to the science: name specific amino acids or the HBV/LBV distinction, give food source examples, and explain the consequence for the body. For “discuss” questions worth 8 marks, make sure you cover both sides — for example, the benefits and drawbacks of protein alternatives — and reach a justified conclusion.

In AQA Food Technology questions about fats or carbohydrates, always be specific about the type (e.g. saturated vs polyunsaturated, monosaccharide vs polysaccharide). Naming specific food sources and linking them to health effects will push your answer into the higher mark bands. For “discuss” questions, consider both positive roles (energy, insulation, vitamins) and negative effects of excess (CHD, obesity, tooth decay) to show balance.

When answering AQA questions about vitamins, always state the specific vitamin, its function, a named food source, and the consequence of deficiency or excess. For example: “Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones. Sources include oily fish and eggs. A deficiency in children causes rickets.” If asked about cooking methods, link your answer to water-soluble vitamin loss and explain how to minimise it (steam, less water, shorter cooking time). For higher-mark questions, always explain the science behind your answer.

before.content_html:
Minerals in the Diet

Minerals are micronutrients that your body needs in small amounts. Unlike vitamins, minerals are inorganic — they come from the soil and water rather than from living things. For your AQA exam, you need to know six minerals: calcium, iron, sodium, fluoride, iodine, and phosphorus.

Calcium

Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body. It is essential for strong bones and teeth, but it also plays a role in muscle contraction, blood clotting, and nerve function. The RNI for adults is 700 mg per day.

Good sources include milk, cheese, yoghurt, green leafy vegetables (such as broccoli and kale), canned fish with bones (like sardines), and fortified foods such as fortified bread and breakfast cereals.

Key Fact

Calcium deficiency causes rickets in children (soft, weak bones that bend) and osteoporosis in adults (brittle bones that fracture easily). Excess calcium can lead to kidney stones.

Iron

Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that transports oxygen around the body. Without enough iron, your cells do not get the oxygen they need, and you feel tired and weak.

There are two types of dietary iron. Haem iron comes from animal sources such as red meat and liver — the body absorbs it easily. Non-haem iron comes from plant sources such as dark green leafy vegetables, beans, nuts, and fortified cereals — it is harder to absorb. Eating vitamin C alongside non-haem iron (for example, a glass of orange juice with a fortified cereal) significantly improves absorption.

Deficiency: Iron deficiency causes anaemia. Symptoms include tiredness, pale skin, and breathlessness. It is one of the most common nutritional deficiencies in the UK, particularly among teenage girls and women of childbearing age.

Excess: Too much iron can cause constipation, nausea, and in severe cases, liver damage. Iron supplements should only be taken on medical advice.

Sodium

Sodium is essential for maintaining fluid balance in the body. It also helps transmit nerve impulses and supports muscle contraction. Most people get sodium from salt (sodium chloride), processed foods, bread, and cheese.

Key Fact

Adults should consume no more than 6 g of salt per day (about one teaspoon). Excess sodium raises blood pressure, increasing the risk of stroke and heart disease. Deficiency is rare but can cause muscle cramps.

Fluoride, Iodine & Phosphorus

Fluoride strengthens tooth enamel and helps prevent dental caries (tooth decay). Sources include fluoridated water, tea, and toothpaste. Many areas in the UK add fluoride to the water supply specifically to reduce tooth decay.

Iodine is needed for the production of thyroid hormones, which control your metabolism. Good sources are seafood, milk, and dairy products. A deficiency causes goitre — a visible swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck.

Phosphorus works alongside calcium to build and maintain strong bones and teeth. It also helps the body release energy from food. Sources include meat, fish, dairy, and cereals. Because it is found in so many foods, deficiency is extremely rare.

Calcium — bones, teeth, blood clotting, muscle contraction. Sources: dairy, leafy greens, fortified foods. Deficiency: rickets/osteoporosis.

Iron — haemoglobin (oxygen transport). Sources: red meat, liver, beans, fortified cereals. Deficiency: anaemia.

Sodium — fluid balance, nerve impulses, muscle contraction. Sources: salt, processed foods. Excess: high blood pressure. Max 6 g salt/day.

Fluoride — tooth enamel, prevents dental caries. Sources: fluoridated water, tea, toothpaste.

Iodine — thyroid hormones, metabolism. Sources: seafood, milk, dairy. Deficiency: goitre.

Phosphorus — bones/teeth (with calcium), energy release. Sources: meat, fish, dairy, cereals.

Water & Hydration

Water is not a mineral, but it is essential for life. Every cell, tissue, and organ in your body needs water to function properly. The specification requires you to understand the functions of water, how it is lost, and how much you need each day.

Waste elimination: Water helps the kidneys flush out waste products through urine.

Temperature regulation: When you are hot, your body produces sweat. As sweat evaporates from the skin, it cools you down.

Digestion: Water is needed to break down food and absorb nutrients in the digestive system.

Nutrient transport: Blood, which is mostly water, carries nutrients and oxygen to cells and removes waste.

Chemical reactions: Many chemical processes in the body, including hydrolysis, require water to take place.

Water is lost continuously through urine, sweat, and breathing. The government recommends drinking 6–8 glasses of fluid per day. Water, lower-fat milk, and sugar-free drinks all count towards this. About 20% of your daily water intake comes from food — soups, yoghurts, fruit, and vegetables all contain significant amounts of water. The remaining 80% should come from drinks.

Key Fact

Fruit juice and smoothies count as a maximum of 150 ml per day combined, no matter how much you drink, because of their high sugar content. Drinking too much water can cause hyponatraemia — dangerously low sodium levels in the blood.

Extra fluids are needed during hot weather, physical activity, illness (especially fever, vomiting, or diarrhoea), and pregnancy or breastfeeding. Dehydration causes headaches, fatigue, poor concentration, and dark-coloured urine. In severe cases it can be life-threatening.
before.exam_tip_html: In AQA Food Technology, “explain” questions about minerals want you to name the mineral, state its function, give food sources, and describe what happens if someone has too little or too much. Always link your answer to a specific group of people where relevant — for example, iron deficiency is particularly common in teenage girls. For “discuss” questions (8 marks), you need to cover multiple minerals or both sides of an argument, and reach a justified conclusion.

before.content_html:
What Is Energy?

Your body needs energy for everything it does — from breathing and pumping blood to walking and exercising. This energy comes from the food and drink you consume. The amount of energy a person needs depends on their age, gender, body size, muscle mass, and how active they are.

Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)

Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) is the amount of energy your body needs just to stay alive when you are completely at rest. It covers essential functions like breathing, keeping your heart beating, maintaining body temperature, and repairing cells. BMR accounts for the largest portion of your daily energy use — typically 60–75% of total energy expenditure.

Age: BMR decreases as you get older because muscle mass naturally declines with age. Younger people have a higher BMR because their bodies are still growing and repairing cells rapidly.

Gender: Males generally have a higher BMR than females because they tend to have more muscle mass. Muscle tissue is metabolically active — it burns energy even at rest.

Body size: A larger body has more cells to maintain, so taller or heavier people typically have a higher BMR than smaller people.

Muscle mass: The more muscle you have, the higher your BMR. This is why athletes and people who exercise regularly burn more energy at rest than sedentary individuals.

Key Fact

BMR is the energy needed for basic functions at complete rest. It is affected by four main factors: age, gender, body size, and muscle mass. A younger, larger, more muscular male will generally have the highest BMR.

Physical Activity Level (PAL)

Physical Activity Level (PAL) is a value that reflects how active a person is during the day. A sedentary office worker has a low PAL (around 1.4), while an athlete or manual labourer has a high PAL (around 2.0 or more). The more active you are, the higher your PAL.

Sedentary (PAL 1.4): Little or no exercise, desk-based work. Examples include office workers or students who do not take part in sport.

Moderately active (PAL 1.6–1.7): Some regular exercise or a job that involves standing and walking. Examples include teachers or shop workers who also exercise a few times a week.

Very active (PAL 1.9–2.0+): Daily vigorous exercise or a physically demanding job. Examples include professional athletes, builders, or farmers.

Calculating Total Energy Needs

To work out how much energy a person needs each day, you multiply their BMR by their PAL:

Key Fact

Total daily energy requirement = BMR × PAL

For example, if a woman has a BMR of 1,400 kcal and a PAL of 1.6 (moderately active), her total daily energy need is 1,400 × 1.6 = 2,240 kcal per day.

Energy Balance

Energy balance is the relationship between the energy you take in from food and the energy your body uses. When energy in equals energy out, your weight stays stable. When they are not equal, your weight changes.

Energy in = Energy out (balanced): Weight stays the same. The person is eating exactly as much energy as they are using. This is the ideal for maintaining a healthy weight.

Energy in > Energy out (surplus): The excess energy is stored as body fat, leading to weight gain. Over time, this can contribute to obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and some cancers.

Energy in < Energy out (deficit): The body uses its stored fat for energy, leading to weight loss. If prolonged, this can cause malnutrition, fatigue, a weakened immune system, and in children it can slow growth and development.

Energy Values of Macronutrients

Different macronutrients provide different amounts of energy per gram. Knowing these values is essential for nutritional analysis and for exam calculations.

4 kcal/g

Protein

Provides 4 kilocalories per gram. Protein is primarily used for growth and repair, but the body can use it for energy when carbohydrate and fat stores are low.

4 kcal/g

Carbohydrate

Provides 4 kilocalories per gram. Carbohydrate is the body’s preferred source of energy, especially for the brain and during exercise.

9 kcal/g

Fat

Provides 9 kilocalories per gram — more than double the energy of protein or carbohydrate. Fat is a concentrated energy source and is stored in the body for use when needed.

7 kcal/g

Alcohol

Provides 7 kilocalories per gram. Alcohol is not a nutrient and has no nutritional benefit, but it does contribute to energy intake.

Key Fact

Energy values you must know: protein = 4 kcal/g, carbohydrate = 4 kcal/g, fat = 9 kcal/g, alcohol = 7 kcal/g. Fat provides more than twice the energy of protein or carbohydrate gram for gram.

Recommended Macronutrient Proportions

The UK government publishes dietary recommendations for how much of each macronutrient should make up a person’s total energy intake. Following these helps reduce the risk of diet-related diseases.

Protein (~15% of total energy): Supports growth, repair, and maintenance of body tissues. Found in meat, fish, eggs, dairy, beans, lentils, and nuts.

Fat (no more than 35% of total energy): Provides essential fatty acids and carries fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Within this, saturated fat should be limited to no more than 11% of total energy to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Carbohydrate (~50% of total energy): The body’s preferred energy source. Of this 50%, around 45% should come from starchy carbohydrates (bread, pasta, rice, potatoes). Free sugars should make up no more than 5% of total energy — about 30g per day for adults.

Nutritional Analysis

Nutritional analysis is the process of working out the nutrient and energy content of a food product or meal. It helps food manufacturers, chefs, and individuals understand what they are eating and whether a dish meets dietary guidelines.

Food composition tables: Published tables such as McCance and Widdowson’s The Composition of Foods list the nutrient content of hundreds of foods per 100g. You look up each ingredient, calculate the amounts used in your recipe, and add them together. This manual method is accurate but time-consuming.

Nutritional analysis software: Programs like Nutritics or MyFitnessPal allow you to enter a recipe and instantly see a full nutritional breakdown. The software compares results against reference intakes and can highlight where a dish is too high in fat, sugar, or salt, or too low in fibre or vitamins.

Food labels: Packaged foods display nutritional information per 100g and per portion. Traffic light labels use red, amber, and green to show whether levels of fat, saturated fat, sugar, and salt are high, medium, or low.

Using Nutritional Analysis to Plan and Modify Dishes

In the exam, you may be asked how nutritional analysis can help you plan, make, or modify a dish. The key idea is that once you know the nutritional profile of a recipe, you can adjust ingredients to make it healthier or to meet a specific dietary need.

Reducing fat: Swap butter for a lower-fat spread, grill instead of fry, use semi-skimmed milk instead of whole milk, or trim visible fat from meat.

Reducing sugar: Use fruit purée to sweeten a cake instead of sugar, reduce the amount of sugar in a recipe by one-third, or choose tinned fruit in juice rather than syrup.

Increasing fibre: Use wholemeal flour instead of white flour, add vegetables or pulses to a sauce or stew, or serve brown rice instead of white rice.

Increasing vitamins and minerals: Add extra vegetables, choose fortified cereals, or include a side salad to boost micronutrient content.

Key Fact

In the exam, always justify modifications using nutritional data. For example: “The analysis showed the dish was high in saturated fat (22g per serving), so I swapped butter for olive oil to reduce it to 8g, bringing the fat content below the 35% guideline.”

flashcard_questions.q: The capacity to do work. In nutrition, energy is measured in kilocalories (kcal) or kilojoules (kJ) and comes from the macronutrients in food.
The amount of energy the body uses at complete rest to maintain basic life functions such as breathing, circulation, and cell repair.
A number that represents how physically active a person is. It is multiplied by BMR to calculate total daily energy needs.
BMR accounts for the largest portion of your daily energy use — typically _____ of total energy expenditure

flashcard_questions.a: The relationship between energy consumed from food and drink (energy in) and energy used by the body for activity and body functions (energy out).

glossary_terms.definition: The capacity to do work. In nutrition, energy is measured in kilocalories (kcal) or kilojoules (kJ) and comes from the macronutrients in food.
The amount of energy the body uses at complete rest to maintain basic life functions such as breathing, circulation, and cell repair.
A number that represents how physically active a person is. It is multiplied by BMR to calculate total daily energy needs.
The relationship between energy consumed from food and drink (energy in) and energy used by the body for activity and body functions (energy out).
A condition where the body does not receive enough nutrients to function properly, resulting from under-eating or a diet lacking essential nutrients.
Nutrients needed in large amounts by the body — protein, carbohydrates, and fats — each providing energy measured in kilocalories per gram.
The process of calculating the nutrient and energy content of a food product or meal using food composition tables or software.
Government guidelines that state how much of each nutrient a person should consume to maintain good health, including reference intakes for energy and individual nutrients.
Fats found mainly in animal products and processed foods. Eating too much raises LDL cholesterol and increases the risk of cardiovascular disease.
Sugars added to foods by manufacturers, cooks, or consumers, plus sugars found naturally in honey, syrups, and fruit juices. The government recommends no more than 5% of energy from free sugars.
The daily amount of a nutrient that is enough to meet the needs of most people in a particular group. Used as a benchmark when assessing nutritional adequacy.

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘obesity’.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for a correct definition:
• A medical condition where a person has a BMI of 30 or above (1), caused by consuming more energy than the body uses over a sustained period (1). Accept either part for full mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe two health risks associated with a diet that is high in saturated fat.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per described health risk (max 2):
• High saturated fat raises blood cholesterol, which increases the risk of coronary heart disease (1).
• Fatty deposits can build up in artery walls, narrowing them and restricting blood flow to the heart (1).
• A high saturated fat diet contributes to obesity, which increases the risk of type 2 diabetes (1).
• Raised cholesterol increases the risk of stroke due to blocked blood vessels in the brain (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lack of iron in the diet can lead to anaemia. In your answer, identify one group of people who are particularly at risk and explain why.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (award up to 4 marks):
• Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen (1).
• Without enough iron, the body cannot produce sufficient haemoglobin, resulting in anaemia (1).
• Symptoms include tiredness, pale skin, breathlessness and difficulty concentrating (1).
• Teenage girls are at risk because they lose iron through menstruation and may not replace it through diet (1).
• Vegetarians/vegans are at risk because plant-based non-haem iron is less easily absorbed than haem iron from animal sources (1).
• Vitamin C aids absorption of non-haem iron (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the dietary causes of coronary heart disease (CHD) and describe how changes to the diet could reduce the risk.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (award up to 6 marks):
• A diet high in saturated fat raises blood cholesterol levels (1).
• Excess cholesterol is deposited on artery walls, forming fatty plaques that narrow the arteries (1).
• A diet high in salt causes water retention, raising blood pressure, which damages artery walls (1).
• Dietary changes: replace saturated fats with unsaturated fats such as olive oil (1).
• Eat oily fish twice a week for omega-3 fatty acids, which protect the heart (1).
• Reduce salt intake to no more than 6g per day by using herbs/spices instead of salt (1).
• Increase soluble fibre from oats, beans and lentils to help lower cholesterol (1).
• Eat at least 5 portions of fruit and vegetables daily (1).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of vitamin D and calcium in the diet across different life stages. Refer to specific health conditions in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Thorough evaluation covering multiple life stages with specific health conditions and a reasoned conclusion.
Indicative content:
• Children need vitamin D and calcium for bone mineralisation. Deficiency causes rickets — soft, weak bones that can become deformed.
• Teenagers need calcium for bone development during growth spurts. Peak bone mass is built during adolescence.
• Adults need to maintain bone density. Adequate calcium intake reduces the risk of fractures later in life.
• Elderly people, particularly post-menopausal women, are at risk of osteoporosis — bones lose density and become brittle, leading to fractures.
• Vitamin D is essential for calcium absorption. Without it, even a calcium-rich diet may not prevent bone disease.
• Sources: dairy products, canned fish with bones, green leafy vegetables (calcium); sunlight, oily fish, eggs, fortified cereals (vitamin D).
• People with darker skin or limited sun exposure need more dietary vitamin D.
• Conclusion: both nutrients are important at every life stage, but the consequences of deficiency are most severe in children (rickets) and elderly people (osteoporosis).
Mid band (4-6): Sound evaluation covering at least two life stages with some specific detail.
Lower band (1-3): Basic points about calcium or vitamin D with limited reference to health conditions.

practice_questions.text: A teenager is eating a diet high in sugary snacks between meals and drinking several cans of fizzy drink each day. Discuss the potential health consequences of this diet and explain what dietary changes you would recommend. You should consider both short-term and long-term effects.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (up to 12 marks + 4 spelling/grammar):

Short-term effects:
• Dental decay — frequent sugar intake feeds bacteria that produce acid, attacking tooth enamel and causing cavities (1–2).
• Energy imbalance — excess sugar provides energy beyond needs, leading to weight gain (1).
• Blood sugar spikes — refined sugars cause rapid rises and falls in blood glucose, leading to energy crashes and poor concentration (1).

Long-term effects:
• Obesity — sustained energy surplus leads to BMI of 30+, increasing risk of CHD, cancers and joint problems (1–2).
• Type 2 diabetes — repeated blood sugar spikes strain insulin response; obesity increases insulin resistance (1–2).
• Coronary heart disease — obesity raises cholesterol and blood pressure (1).

Dietary recommendations:
• Replace fizzy drinks with water, milk or sugar-free alternatives (1).
• Swap sugary snacks for fruit, nuts or wholegrain options (1).
• Reduce frequency of sugar consumption rather than just total amount, to limit acid attacks on teeth (1).
• Follow the Eatwell Guide — free sugars should be no more than 5% of total energy (about 30g per day) (1).
• Include regular meals with complex carbohydrates for steady energy release (1).

spelling/grammar (4 marks): Spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of specialist terminology.

before.content_html:
What Is Food Spoilage?

Food spoilage is the process by which food deteriorates and becomes unfit to eat. It is caused by the growth of bacteria, moulds, and yeasts. These are all types of micro-organisms — they are too small to see without a microscope, but their effects on food are very visible.

Bacteria are the most dangerous because they can cause food poisoning. Moulds grow on the surface of food and produce visible fuzzy patches. Yeasts ferment sugars in food, producing carbon dioxide and alcohol, which changes the taste and smell.

Key Fact

Not all micro-organisms are harmful. Some bacteria are used to make yoghurt and cheese. Yeast is essential for bread-making. Moulds give blue cheese its flavour. The difference is whether their growth is controlled or uncontrolled.

Signs of Food Spoilage

You can detect spoiled food using your senses. The main signs are:

Colour changes — meat may turn grey or green, bread may develop blue or white spots, and fruit may turn brown. Texture changes — food becomes slimy, soft, or mushy when bacteria break down its structure. Smell — spoiled food often produces a sour, rancid, or “off” odour as micro-organisms release waste products. Taste — food tastes sour, bitter, or fermented (though you should never taste food you suspect is spoiled). Visible mould — fuzzy patches of white, green, blue, or black growth appear on the surface.

Key Fact

Pathogenic bacteria do not cause visible signs of spoilage. Food can look, smell, and taste perfectly normal but still contain dangerous levels of harmful bacteria. This is why food safety rules matter even when food appears fine.

Conditions for Bacterial Growth

Bacteria need specific conditions to multiply. If any of these conditions are removed, bacterial growth slows down or stops. You can remember them using the mnemonic FATTOM: Food, Acidity, Time, Temperature, Oxygen, Moisture.

Food — bacteria need nutrients to grow. High-protein foods like meat, dairy, and eggs are ideal. These are called high-risk foods.

Acidity (pH) — most bacteria prefer neutral pH (around 7). Acidic conditions (low pH) slow growth, which is why vinegar and lemon juice are used as preservatives.

Time — in ideal conditions, bacteria can divide every 10–20 minutes. A single bacterium can become millions within just a few hours. This is called binary fission.

Temperature — bacteria multiply fastest between 5°C and 63°C. This range is called the danger zone. Below 5°C, growth slows dramatically. Above 63°C, most bacteria are killed. Food must be kept out of the danger zone as much as possible.

Oxygen — most food-poisoning bacteria are aerobic (they need oxygen). However, some are anaerobic and can grow without oxygen, such as Clostridium perfringens in vacuum-packed foods.

Moisture — bacteria need water to grow. Dried foods like pasta, rice, and flour have very low moisture content, so bacteria cannot multiply. This is why drying is an effective preservation method.

Enzymic Browning

Enzymic browning is a type of food spoilage caused by enzymes, not micro-organisms. When fruit or vegetables are cut, enzymes inside the cells react with oxygen in the air. This causes the surface to turn brown — think of a sliced apple left on a worktop.

You can prevent enzymic browning in three ways: add acid (lemon juice lowers the pH and slows the enzyme reaction), blanching (briefly plunging food into boiling water destroys the enzymes), or excluding air (submerging food in water or wrapping tightly prevents oxygen reaching the surface).

Types of Contamination

Food contamination means that something unwanted or harmful has entered the food. There are four types, and the exam may ask you to give examples of each.

Microbiological contamination — caused by bacteria, viruses, moulds, or parasites entering food. This is the most common cause of food poisoning. Examples include Salmonella from raw chicken and E. coli from undercooked beef.

Chemical contamination — caused by cleaning products, pesticides, or other chemicals coming into contact with food. For example, storing food in containers previously used for chemicals, or not rinsing surfaces after using antibacterial spray.

Physical contamination — caused by foreign objects entering food, such as hair, glass, plasters, packaging, insects, or pieces of equipment. This can cause choking, broken teeth, or cuts.

Allergenic contamination — caused by allergens being accidentally transferred into food. For example, using the same knife to cut a nut cake and then a plain cake. The 14 major allergens must be declared by law in the UK.

Cross-Contamination

Cross-contamination is the transfer of harmful bacteria from one food or surface to another. It is one of the most common causes of food poisoning in the home and in commercial kitchens.

The main routes of cross-contamination are: hands — touching raw meat then handling ready-to-eat food without washing hands; chopping boards — using the same board for raw chicken and salad; utensils — using the same knife for raw and cooked food; cloths — wiping surfaces with a dirty cloth spreads bacteria; and dripping — raw meat juices dripping onto ready-to-eat food below in the fridge.

Key Fact

In the exam, always store raw meat on the bottom shelf of the fridge to prevent juices dripping onto other foods. Use colour-coded chopping boards: red for raw meat, green for salad and vegetables, blue for raw fish, yellow for cooked meat.

High-Risk Foods

High-risk foods are ready-to-eat foods that are high in protein and moisture. Because they will not be cooked again before eating, any bacteria present will not be destroyed. Examples include: cooked meat and poultry, dairy products (milk, cream, soft cheese), cooked rice (Bacillus cereus produces toxins in reheated rice), shellfish, eggs and egg products (mayonnaise, custard).

Key Pathogenic Bacteria

You need to know six key pathogens for the exam, including where they are found and how to prevent them.

Salmonella — found in raw poultry, eggs, and raw meat. Causes vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, and abdominal cramps. Prevented by thorough cooking (core temperature 75°C) and avoiding raw egg in uncooked dishes.

E. coli (O157) — found in undercooked beef, raw milk, and contaminated water. Can cause severe bloody diarrhoea and kidney failure. Prevented by cooking minced beef thoroughly and avoiding cross-contamination.

Campylobacter — the most common cause of food poisoning in the UK. Found on raw poultry. Causes diarrhoea (often bloody), cramping, and fever. Prevented by not washing raw chicken (which splashes bacteria) and cooking poultry to 75°C.

Staphylococcus aureus — carried on the skin, in the nose, and in infected cuts of food handlers. Transferred to food by coughing, sneezing, or touching food with unwashed hands. Prevented by good personal hygiene, covering cuts with blue waterproof plasters, and not handling food when ill.

Listeria — found in soft cheeses (Brie, Camembert), pâté, and ready-to-eat salads. Unlike most bacteria, Listeria can grow at fridge temperatures (below 5°C). Particularly dangerous for pregnant women. Prevented by avoiding high-risk chilled foods and checking use-by dates.

Clostridium perfringens — found in soil, dust, and the intestines of animals. Causes illness when food (especially meat and poultry) is cooked, cooled too slowly, and then reheated. The bacterium forms heat-resistant spores. Prevented by cooling food quickly (within 90 minutes) and reheating to at least 75°C.

Symptoms of Food Poisoning

Food poisoning symptoms typically appear 1–72 hours after eating contaminated food. The most common symptoms are: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, and fever. In severe cases, food poisoning can cause dehydration, kidney failure, and even death.

Vulnerable Groups

Some people are more vulnerable to food poisoning because their immune systems are weaker. These at-risk groups include: young children (underdeveloped immune system), elderly people (declining immune function), pregnant women (Listeria and Salmonella are particularly dangerous and can harm the unborn baby), and immunocompromised individuals (people with conditions like HIV/AIDS or those undergoing chemotherapy).

Young children have immune systems that are still developing, so they cannot fight off infections as effectively as adults. Elderly people experience natural decline in immune function, and they may also be dehydrated or malnourished, which makes recovery harder. Pregnant women’s immune systems are naturally suppressed to protect the baby, which makes them more susceptible to infections like Listeria. Immunocompromised individuals have weakened immune defences due to illness or medical treatment, so even small amounts of bacteria can cause serious illness.

glossary_terms.definition: The process by which food deteriorates in quality, becoming unfit or unpleasant to eat.
Single-celled micro-organisms that multiply rapidly in warm, moist conditions and can cause food poisoning.
A type of fungus that grows on food surfaces, producing visible fuzzy patches and releasing spores into the air.
Single-celled fungi used in baking and brewing, but which can also cause food spoilage by fermenting sugars.
Tiny living organisms, including bacteria, moulds and yeasts, that are too small to see without a microscope.
Harmful bacteria that cause illness but do not change the appearance, smell, or taste of food.
Foods that are ready to eat, high in protein, and moist, making them ideal for bacterial growth. Examples include cooked meat, dairy products, and cooked rice.
The rapid increase in bacterial numbers that occurs when conditions are favourable, with cells dividing every 10 to 20 minutes.
The temperature range between 5 and 63 degrees Celsius in which bacteria multiply most rapidly.
A chemical reaction that occurs when enzymes in cut fruit and vegetables are exposed to oxygen, causing the surface to turn brown.
The presence of unwanted or harmful substances in food that make it unsafe to eat.
Substances found in food that trigger an immune response in sensitive individuals, such as nuts, milk, eggs, or gluten.
The transfer of harmful bacteria or other contaminants from one food, surface, or piece of equipment to another.
Disease-causing bacteria that can multiply in food and produce toxins, leading to food poisoning.
An illness caused by eating food contaminated with pathogenic bacteria, viruses, or their toxins.
Groups of people who are more susceptible to food poisoning due to weaker immune systems, including young children, the elderly, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'danger zone' in relation to food safety.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for: The temperature range between 5°C and 63°C (1) in which bacteria multiply most rapidly (1).

Accept: The range of temperatures where bacteria grow fastest / where food is unsafe.

practice_questions.text: Describe two signs that food has become spoiled.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each valid sign described, up to 2 marks.
• Colour changes, e.g. meat turning grey/green (1)
• Texture becomes slimy or mushy (1)
• Unpleasant/sour/rancid smell (1)
• Sour or fermented taste (1)
• Visible mould growth on the surface (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how cross-contamination can occur when preparing a meal that includes raw chicken and a side salad.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each valid explanation point, up to 4 marks.
• Using the same chopping board for raw chicken and salad vegetables transfers bacteria such as Campylobacter/Salmonella (1)
• Not washing hands after handling raw chicken and then touching salad ingredients (1)
• Using the same knife for raw chicken and then for cutting salad (1)
• Wiping surfaces with a contaminated cloth then placing salad on that surface (1)
• Splashing raw chicken juices onto salad when washing chicken under a tap (1)
• Raw chicken stored above salad in the fridge, allowing juices to drip down (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how the conditions needed for bacterial growth can be controlled to keep food safe. Refer to at least three conditions in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for identification of conditions AND explanation of how they are controlled.

• Temperature — keep food out of the danger zone (5–63°C) by refrigerating below 5°C or cooking above 75°C (1–2)
• Moisture — remove moisture through drying, salting, or adding sugar to preserve food (1–2)
• Time — limit the time food spends in the danger zone; cool cooked food within 90 minutes (1–2)
• pH/Acidity — lower pH using vinegar or lemon juice to create conditions bacteria cannot thrive in (1–2)
• Oxygen — vacuum packing removes oxygen to slow aerobic bacterial growth (1–2)
• Food/nutrients — keep high-risk foods refrigerated and separate from raw foods (1–2)

Maximum 6 marks. At least three conditions must be addressed for full marks.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of personal hygiene for food handlers in preventing food contamination. In your answer, refer to specific bacteria and types of contamination.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Thorough evaluation with specific named bacteria and types of contamination. Clear judgement on the importance of personal hygiene with well-developed reasoning. E.g. Staphylococcus aureus is carried on the skin, in the nose, and in infected cuts — food handlers who do not wash hands, cover cuts with blue waterproof plasters, or wear hairnets risk transferring bacteria (microbiological contamination) and hair/plasters (physical contamination) to food. Cross-contamination is a leading cause of food poisoning. However, personal hygiene alone is not enough — correct storage temperatures, thorough cooking, and preventing chemical contamination are equally important.
Mid band (4-6): Some relevant points with at least one named bacterium. Attempts evaluation but may lack detail or not cover all contamination types.
Lower band (1-3): Basic points about washing hands or wearing aprons. Limited or no reference to specific bacteria or types of contamination.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the risks of food poisoning for vulnerable groups. Explain why these groups are more at risk and what precautions should be taken when preparing food for them.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive discussion identifying all four vulnerable groups (young children, elderly, pregnant women, immunocompromised) with detailed explanations of why each is at risk. Specific precautions linked to named pathogens. E.g. Pregnant women should avoid soft cheeses like Brie because Listeria can grow at fridge temperatures and may cause miscarriage. Young children have underdeveloped immune systems, so food must be cooked to a core temperature of 75°C. Elderly people may become dehydrated more quickly from vomiting/diarrhoea. Precautions: thorough cooking, strict date checking, avoiding high-risk foods, preventing cross-contamination.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Developed discussion covering at least three vulnerable groups with some specific pathogens and precautions.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some knowledge of vulnerable groups and basic precautions. Limited reference to specific bacteria.
Lower band (1-3): Simple identification of one or two groups with basic reasoning.
spelling/grammar: 4 marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar, and use of specialist terminology.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Personal hygiene rules — handwashing, tied hair, clean apron, blue plasters, no sneezing over food, and the 48-hour rule — prevent bacteria from food handlers reaching food.
  • Kitchen hygiene relies on cleaning as you go, using antibacterial products, colour-coded chopping boards (red = raw meat, blue = fish, yellow = cooked meat, green = veg, white = bakery, brown = fruit), washing cloths at 60°C, and using foot-operated bins.
  • Critical temperatures: fridge 0–5°C (raw meat on bottom), freezer −18°C, core cooking 75°C for 2 minutes, hot holding 63°C, cool within 90 minutes, reheat once only. Use-by = safety, best-before = quality, display-until = shop only.
before.content_html:
Why Food Hygiene Matters

Good food hygiene prevents contamination and food poisoning. Every year in the UK, around one million people suffer from foodborne illness — most cases are caused by poor hygiene during preparation, storage, or cooking. For the exam , you need to know the hygiene rules that apply to people, kitchens, storage, and cooking temperatures.

Food hygiene covers four main areas: personal hygiene (what the food handler does), kitchen hygiene (how the workspace is kept clean), food storage (how food is kept at safe temperatures), and cooking and temperature control (how food is heated, held, cooled, and reheated safely).

Personal Hygiene

Anyone handling food must follow strict personal hygiene rules to prevent bacteria from their body, clothing, or habits from contaminating the food.

  • Wash hands thoroughly — use hot water and antibacterial soap for at least 20 seconds before handling food, after touching raw food, after using the toilet, after sneezing or coughing, and after handling waste. Proper handwashing is the single most important step in preventing cross-contamination.
  • Tie hair back — long hair must be tied back and ideally covered with a hairnet or hat to prevent loose hairs falling into food (physical contamination).
  • Wear a clean apron — protects food from bacteria on outdoor clothing and protects the handler from splashes. Aprons should be changed if they become soiled.
  • Use blue plasters — any cuts or sores on the hands must be covered with a blue plaster. Blue is used because no natural food is blue, so a fallen plaster is easy to spot. In commercial kitchens, these plasters often contain a metal strip so they can be detected by metal detectors on production lines.
  • No sneezing or coughing over food — Staphylococcus aureus lives in the nose and throat. Sneezing or coughing near food can spray thousands of bacteria onto it. If you need to sneeze, turn away from the food and wash your hands afterwards.
  • Follow the 48-hour rule — food handlers should not prepare food for others for at least 48 hours after the last episode of vomiting or diarrhoea. This prevents the spread of norovirus and other foodborne infections to others.
Key Fact

The 48-hour rule means a food handler must wait 48 hours after symptoms of vomiting or diarrhoea have stopped before returning to work. This is a legal requirement under food safety regulations and applies in schools, restaurants, and food factories.

Kitchen Hygiene

A clean, well-organised kitchen reduces the risk of cross-contamination. Good kitchen hygiene is about preventing bacteria from building up on surfaces, equipment, and cloths.

Clean as you go: Wipe down surfaces, wash up equipment, and put away ingredients as you work rather than leaving everything until the end. This prevents bacteria from multiplying on dirty surfaces and reduces the risk of cross-contamination between tasks.

Use antibacterial spray or sanitiser: Work surfaces must be cleaned with an antibacterial cleaning product before and after food preparation, especially after contact with raw meat. Standard washing-up liquid removes visible dirt but does not kill bacteria — an antibacterial product is needed.

Colour-coded chopping boards: Different coloured boards are used for different food types to prevent cross-contamination. This system is a legal requirement in commercial kitchens and strongly recommended in school and home kitchens.

Wash cloths and tea towels at 60°C: Kitchen cloths and tea towels harbour bacteria quickly. They must be washed at 60°C or above to kill harmful bacteria. Ideally, use disposable cloths or replace reusable ones daily.

Use foot-operated bins: Bins with foot-operated lids prevent food handlers from touching the bin lid with their hands, which would transfer bacteria back to the food. Bins should be emptied regularly and lined with a bin bag.

Key Fact — Colour-Coded Chopping Boards

The standard colour-coding system is: Red = raw meat, Blue = raw fish, Yellow = cooked meat, Green = salad & vegetables, White = bakery & dairy, Brown = raw vegetables & fruit. Using the correct board for each food type prevents bacteria from raw foods being transferred to ready-to-eat foods.

Food Storage

Correct storage keeps food out of the danger zone (5–63°C) and prevents cross-contamination. There are three main types of storage: refrigeration, freezing, and dry (ambient) storage.

Refrigerator (0–5°C): The fridge must be kept between 0°C and 5°C. Store raw meat on the bottom shelf so that juices cannot drip down onto ready-to-eat food below. Ready-to-eat food, dairy, and cooked leftovers go on upper shelves. Cover all food to prevent drying out and to reduce the risk of cross-contamination. Check the fridge temperature regularly with a thermometer.

Freezer (−18°C or below): A freezer should operate at −18°C or below. Freezing does not kill bacteria — it stops them multiplying by removing available water. Once food is thawed, bacteria become active again, which is why frozen food must be defrosted thoroughly (ideally in the fridge) and cooked immediately. Food should never be refrozen once thawed unless it has been cooked first.

Dry (ambient) storage — FIFO: Dry stores hold tinned, packaged, and dried goods at room temperature. They must be clean, cool, dry, and well-ventilated. Stock should be rotated using the FIFO (First In, First Out) system: place new deliveries at the back and bring older stock to the front so the oldest items are used first. This prevents food going past its date.

Cooking & Temperature Control

Temperature control is the most effective way to make food safe. Bacteria are killed at high temperatures, and their growth is slowed or stopped at very low temperatures. For the exam, you must know the critical temperatures and rules.

  • Core temperature of 75°C for 2 minutes: When cooking, the centre (core) of the food must reach at least 75°C for at least 2 minutes to kill harmful bacteria such as Salmonella and E. coli. Use a temperature probe pushed into the thickest part of the food to check.
  • Hot holding at 63°C: Food displayed on a buffet or carvery must be kept at 63°C or above to stay out of the danger zone. If it drops below this, it must be discarded or rapidly reheated.
  • Cool within 90 minutes: After cooking, if food is not being served immediately, it must be cooled to below 5°C within 90 minutes. This minimises the time food spends in the danger zone. Use shallow containers, blast chillers, or an ice bath to cool food quickly.
  • Reheat only once: Food should be reheated only once to a core temperature of at least 75°C. Each time food is cooled and reheated, it passes through the danger zone, giving bacteria a chance to multiply. Repeated reheating increases the risk of food poisoning.
  • Use a temperature probe: A temperature probe is the only reliable way to check that food has reached a safe core temperature. The probe must be cleaned and sanitised between uses to avoid cross-contamination. Insert it into the thickest or densest part of the food.
Key Fact — Critical Temperatures

−18°C = freezer (bacteria dormant). 0–5°C = fridge (bacteria growth very slow). 5–63°C = danger zone (bacteria multiply rapidly). 63°C = hot holding minimum. 75°C for 2 minutes = safe core cooking temperature. 100°C = boiling point of water. Learn these numbers — they appear in almost every food hygiene exam question.

Date Markings on Food

Food labels carry date markings that tell consumers and food handlers when food is safe to eat. The specification requires you to understand the difference between three types of date.

Use-by date: This is a safety date. It appears on perishable, high-risk foods such as meat, fish, dairy, and ready meals. After the use-by date, the food may contain harmful levels of bacteria even if it looks and smells normal. It is illegal for shops to sell food past its use-by date, and food handlers must discard it.

Best-before date: This is a quality date. It appears on longer-lasting foods such as canned goods, dried pasta, biscuits, and frozen food. After the best-before date, the food is still safe to eat but may not be at its best in terms of taste, texture, or appearance. Shops can legally sell food past its best-before date.

Display-until date: This is a shop-only date used by retailers for stock control. It tells shop staff when to remove products from the shelves. It has no legal food safety meaning for consumers and is often removed or not printed on smaller products.

Use-by = safety. Found on high-risk perishable foods. Must not be eaten after this date. Illegal to sell past this date. Best-before = quality. Found on longer-lasting foods. Safe to eat after this date but quality may decline. Legal to sell past this date. Display-until = stock control only. Used by shops to manage shelf displays. No legal meaning for consumers.
before.exam_tip_html: When AQA asks you to “explain” a food hygiene practice, always link the action to the reason. For example: “Raw meat should be stored on the bottom shelf of the fridge because if juices drip onto ready-to-eat food below, bacteria such as Salmonella could cause cross-contamination and food poisoning.” Naming a specific bacterium and a specific food lifts your answer from Level 1 to Level 2. For 8-mark “discuss” questions on hygiene, organise your answer by area (personal, kitchen, storage, cooking) rather than writing a long unstructured list.

before.content_html:
What Influences Food Choice?

People do not simply eat whatever is available — their food choices are shaped by a wide range of factors. For the exam , you need to understand why individuals and groups choose certain foods and avoid others. These factors fall into several categories: personal preferences, practical considerations, religion, medical needs, and ethical beliefs.

Key Fact

The main factors influencing food choice are: enjoyment, culture and tradition, season and availability, cost, time of day, activity level, religion, medical conditions, ethical beliefs, and marketing. The exam may ask you to explain how any of these factors affect what people eat.

Personal & Practical Factors

Enjoyment is the most basic driver of food choice — people eat foods they find pleasurable. This is closely linked to sensory analysis, which considers how food appeals to our senses: appearance (colour, shape, presentation), aroma (smell), taste (sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami), texture (crunchy, smooth, chewy), and sound (the crunch of a crisp, the sizzle of a stir-fry).

Culture and tradition play a huge role. A traditional British Sunday roast, a Chinese New Year banquet, or an Indian Diwali celebration all involve specific foods tied to cultural identity. Many people eat the foods they grew up with because of family habits and traditions.

Season and availability affect what is fresh, local, and affordable. Strawberries are cheaper and tastier in summer; root vegetables like parsnips are at their best in winter. Seasonal eating also reduces food miles and environmental impact.

Cost is a major factor for many families. Processed and convenience foods are often cheaper per calorie than fresh fruit and vegetables, which is one reason why low-income households may have less varied diets. Special offers and budget brands influence choices.

Time of day and activity level also matter. A builder doing heavy physical work needs more energy-dense food than an office worker. Breakfast foods differ from evening meals. Athletes may eat high-carbohydrate meals before training to maximise glycogen stores.

Marketing and advertising have a powerful influence, especially on young people. Packaging design, celebrity endorsements, social media campaigns, and product placement can all shape what consumers buy. This is why there are restrictions on advertising high fat, salt, and sugar (HFSS) foods to children.

Religious Dietary Requirements

Many religions have specific rules about what followers can and cannot eat. Food preparers must understand these requirements to cater for diverse communities.

Islam (Halal) — Muslims eat only halal food. Pork and its by-products are strictly forbidden (haram). Animals must be slaughtered according to Islamic law, with a prayer recited and the blood drained. Alcohol is also prohibited.

Judaism (Kosher) — Jewish dietary laws (kosher) forbid pork and shellfish. Meat and dairy products must never be prepared, cooked, or eaten together — separate utensils, pans, and even sinks are used. Animals must be slaughtered by a trained person (shochet) with a single cut.

Hinduism — many Hindus are vegetarian because of the principle of ahimsa (non-violence). The cow is considered sacred, so beef is never eaten. Those who do eat meat avoid beef and may also avoid pork. Fasting is common on certain holy days.

Sikhism — some Sikhs are vegetarian, while others eat meat but avoid beef and may avoid pork. Food served in the Gurdwara (Sikh temple) is always vegetarian so that everyone can eat together regardless of their personal dietary choice. This communal meal is called langar.

Medical Dietary Needs

Some people must follow specific diets for medical reasons. Getting these wrong can cause serious illness or even death.

Coeliac disease — an autoimmune condition triggered by gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. People with coeliac disease must follow a strict gluten-free diet. Even small traces of gluten damage the lining of the small intestine, leading to bloating, diarrhoea, weight loss, and poor absorption of nutrients. Gluten-free alternatives include rice, potatoes, corn, and oats (if certified gluten-free).

Lactose intolerance — the body cannot digest lactose, the natural sugar in milk and dairy products. Symptoms include bloating, stomach cramps, and diarrhoea. Lactose-free milk, plant-based milks (soya, oat, almond), and hard cheeses (which are lower in lactose) are suitable alternatives.

Nut allergy — one of the most dangerous food allergies. Even tiny amounts of tree nuts or peanuts can trigger anaphylaxis — a life-threatening reaction causing swelling of the throat, breathing difficulties, and a drop in blood pressure. People with nut allergies carry an adrenaline auto-injector (EpiPen). Food labels must clearly declare nuts as one of the 14 major allergens.

Key Fact

The three medical conditions you must know for AQA are coeliac disease (no gluten), lactose intolerance (no lactose/dairy), and nut allergy (can cause anaphylaxis). For each one, know the cause, the symptoms, and suitable food alternatives.

Ethical & Environmental Food Choices

An increasing number of consumers make food choices based on ethical beliefs about animal welfare, the environment, and fair treatment of workers.

  • Vegetarian — does not eat meat or fish. Eats dairy products and eggs. Motivations include animal welfare, health, and environmental concerns.
  • Vegan — does not eat any animal products at all (no meat, fish, dairy, eggs, or honey). Vegans often also avoid non-food animal products such as leather.
  • Organic — produced without artificial pesticides, fertilisers, or genetically modified organisms (GMOs). Organic food is certified by bodies like the Soil Association. It is typically more expensive.
  • Fairtrade — products guarantee farmers in developing countries receive a fair price. Common Fairtrade items include bananas, coffee, chocolate, and tea.
  • Free-range — animals have access to outdoor space, which improves animal welfare. Free-range eggs and chicken are common examples.
  • Food miles — the distance food travels from producer to consumer. Locally sourced food has fewer food miles, reducing carbon emissions from transport. Seasonal eating also reduces the need for long-distance imports.
  • Sustainability — choosing foods produced in ways that protect the environment for future generations, such as sustainably caught fish (MSC certified) or food with minimal packaging.

Food Labelling

Food labelling is governed by UK and EU law. Labels give consumers the information they need to make safe and informed choices. There are mandatory requirements — things that must appear on every pre-packed food label by law.

By law, every pre-packed food must display:

  • Name of the food — must accurately describe the product (e.g. “strawberry flavour yoghurt” if it contains no real strawberries)
  • Ingredients list — listed in descending order of weight, so the first ingredient is the one present in the largest amount
  • Allergen declaration — the 14 major allergens must be highlighted in bold, italics, or CAPITALS within the ingredients list
  • Net quantity — the weight (grams/kilograms) or volume (millilitres/litres) of the product
  • Date marking — “use by” dates for safety (must not be eaten after this date) and “best before” dates for quality (safe but may not be at best quality)
  • Storage conditions — how to store the product (e.g. “keep refrigerated below 5°C”)
  • Manufacturer/packer name and address — so consumers know who made the product
  • Country of origin — required for certain foods such as beef, fish, honey, olive oil, and fresh fruit/vegetables
  • Nutrition information — a panel showing energy (kJ/kcal), fat, saturated fat, carbohydrate, sugars, protein, and salt per 100g and per serving
  • Cooking/preparation instructions — where necessary for safe consumption

The 14 Major Allergens

UK law requires that 14 specific allergens are clearly declared on food labels whenever they are used as ingredients. These allergens must be emphasised (usually in bold) in the ingredients list so that people with allergies can quickly identify them.

Key Fact — The 14 Allergens

The 14 major allergens are: celery, cereals containing gluten (wheat, barley, rye, oats), crustaceans (prawns, crab, lobster), eggs, fish, lupin, milk, molluscs (mussels, squid, snails), mustard, tree nuts (almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, cashews, pecans, brazils, pistachios, macadamias), peanuts, sesame, soya, and sulphur dioxide/sulphites. You must be able to list these For the exam .

Traffic Light Labelling & Nutrition Panels

The traffic light system is a voluntary front-of-pack labelling scheme used in the UK. It uses red, amber, and green colour coding to show at a glance whether a food is high, medium, or low in four key nutrients: fat, saturated fat, sugar, and salt.

  • Red — high in this nutrient. Eat these foods less often or in small amounts.
  • Amber — medium. An acceptable choice most of the time.
  • Green — low in this nutrient. A healthier choice.

The mandatory nutrition panel on the back of pack shows values per 100g (for comparison between products) and per serving (to show what you actually get in a portion). It includes energy (in kJ and kcal), fat, saturated fat, carbohydrate, sugars, protein, and salt.

Reference Intakes (RIs) are guidelines showing the maximum amount of energy and nutrients an average adult should consume daily. They are based on a 2,000 kcal diet for an average woman. Labels often show each nutrient as a percentage of the RI, helping consumers judge how a product fits into their overall daily diet.

Key Fact — Health Claims

Health claims on food packaging (e.g. “helps maintain normal blood cholesterol”) must be authorised and scientifically proven before they can appear. Manufacturers cannot make unproven health claims. Nutrition claims like “low fat” or “high fibre” also have legally defined thresholds — a product labelled “low fat” must contain no more than 3g of fat per 100g.

lessons.title: Food Science — Heat Transfer and Functional Properties

before.exam_tip_html: Questions on food science are common in Section B of the AQA Food Preparation and Nutrition exam. When asked to explain a functional property, always name the property, describe what happens at a molecular level, and give a specific food example. For instance, “Gelatinisation occurs when starch granules absorb water and swell on heating, eventually bursting to thicken the liquid — this is how a roux sauce thickens.” In longer questions about cooking methods, always link the method to its heat transfer type (conduction, convection, or radiation) and explain how it affects the nutritive value of the food.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'denaturation' in relation to protein.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for: The process by which the structure of a protein molecule is changed (1) by heat, acid, or agitation, causing it to unwind and lose its original shape (1).

Accept: Protein molecules uncoil/change shape when heated or exposed to acid.

practice_questions.text: Explain how gelatinisation occurs when making a sauce.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each valid point, up to 2 marks.
• Starch granules absorb water/liquid when heated (1)
• Granules swell and eventually burst (1)
• Starch molecules are released into the liquid, causing it to thicken (1)
• The ratio of starch to liquid determines the final viscosity/thickness (1)

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between conduction and convection as methods of heat transfer.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each correct description, up to 2 marks.
• Conduction: heat is transferred through direct contact/from molecule to molecule through a solid (1)
• Convection: heat is transferred through a liquid or gas as warm particles rise and cool particles sink, creating circular currents (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain the function of fat in making shortcrust pastry, and why the pastry has a crumbly texture.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each valid point, up to 4 marks.
• Fat is rubbed into flour (1)
• Fat coats the flour particles (1)
• This prevents long gluten strands from forming (1)
• The result is a short/crumbly texture (1)
• Butter/lard/margarine are suitable shortening fats (1)
• The ratio of fat to flour affects how crumbly the pastry is (1)

practice_questions.text: Compare steaming and boiling as methods of cooking vegetables. Explain which method better conserves the nutritive value of the vegetables.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (award marks across Level 1–3):
Top band (5-6): Detailed comparison with clear reasoning.
• Boiling submerges food in water at 100°C; steaming uses steam from boiling water below
• In boiling, water-soluble vitamins (B and C) leach/dissolve into the cooking water and are lost
• In steaming, food does not touch the water so fewer vitamins are lost
• Steaming better conserves nutritive value because there is minimal contact with water
• Steaming also retains colour and texture better
Mid band (3-4): Sound comparison with some reasoning.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points with limited comparison.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the role of raising agents in baking. In your answer, refer to chemical, mechanical, and biological raising agents, giving examples of products that use each type.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (award marks across Level 1–3):
Top band (5-6): Detailed discussion with specific examples.
• Chemical: baking powder/bicarb produce CO₂ when heated/moistened — used in cakes, scones
• Mechanical: whisking/creaming/sieving trap air — used in meringues, creamed cakes
• Biological: yeast ferments sugar to produce CO₂ and alcohol — used in bread
• Steam: water turns to steam and expands — used in choux pastry, Yorkshire puddings
• Explains how each type introduces gas that expands during baking
Mid band (3-4): Sound discussion with some examples.
Lower band (1-2): Basic understanding with limited examples.

lessons.title: Food Provenance — Sustainability, Processing and Production

before.content_html:
Where Does Our Food Come From?

Every ingredient has a journey from food provenance to your plate. Understanding where food comes from — and how it is produced — is essential for making informed, sustainable choices. Food is grown (crops, fruit, vegetables), reared (livestock for meat, eggs, dairy), or caught (fish, shellfish).

The way food is produced varies widely. Organic farming avoids synthetic pesticides and fertilisers, relying on crop rotation, composting, and natural pest control. It is seen as better for the environment and animal welfare, but produces lower yields and costs more. Conventional farming uses chemical inputs to maximise yield, keeping prices lower but raising concerns about chemical residues and environmental damage.

Key Fact

Organic farming: no synthetic pesticides or fertilisers, better for biodiversity, higher animal welfare standards, but lower yields and higher prices. Conventional farming: higher yields, cheaper food, more widely available, but concerns about chemical residues, soil degradation, and lower animal welfare in intensive systems.

Free-range farming gives animals access to outdoor space and the freedom to exhibit natural behaviours. Intensive farming (factory farming) confines large numbers of animals in small spaces to maximise output. Free-range products cost more but are considered more ethical. Sustainable fishing aims to maintain fish populations by avoiding overfishing, using methods like line-caught fishing rather than large-scale trawling, and respecting quotas.

Local, Seasonal, and GM Foods

Local food is produced and sold within a short distance. Advantages: fresher, supports local economy, lower food miles, fewer preservatives needed. Disadvantages: limited variety (especially in winter), may cost more, smaller-scale production.

Seasonal food is grown and harvested at its natural time of year in a particular region. Advantages: better flavour, cheaper (greater supply), lower environmental impact. Disadvantages: limited availability, consumers accustomed to year-round supply may resist.

Genetically modified (GM) food has had its DNA altered to introduce desirable traits, such as pest resistance, higher yields, or improved nutritional content. Advantages: can increase food production, reduce pesticide use, improve nutritional value (e.g. golden rice). Disadvantages: concerns about long-term health effects, cross-pollination with wild plants, ethical objections, labelling requirements in the EU/UK.

Environmental Impact of Food Production

Food miles measure the distance food travels from production to consumption. High food miles mean more transport emissions, contributing to a larger carbon footprint. However, food miles alone are not the full picture — a product grown in a heated UK greenhouse may have a higher carbon footprint than the same product grown outdoors in a warmer country and shipped by sea.

Packaging waste is a major environmental issue. Excessive plastic packaging ends up in landfill or pollutes oceans. Solutions include using recyclable or biodegradable packaging, buying loose produce, and reusing containers. Food waste occurs at every stage of the supply chain — from farms (cosmetically imperfect produce discarded) to households (buying too much, poor storage). Reducing food waste saves money and reduces greenhouse gas emissions from decomposing food in landfill.

Key Fact

Consumers can reduce environmental impact by: buying local and seasonal food (lower food miles), reducing packaging waste (choosing recyclable options), minimising food waste (meal planning, proper storage), and choosing sustainably sourced products (MSC-certified fish, Fairtrade goods).

Food Security and Sustainability

Food security means all people having access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food at all times. Globally, food security is threatened by: a growing population (expected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050), climate change (droughts, flooding, unpredictable seasons), insufficient agricultural land (urbanisation reduces farmland), and water scarcity.

Sustainability in food production means meeting current needs without compromising future generations. Strategies include: reducing food waste, sustainable farming practices, developing drought-resistant crops, and improving food distribution systems.

Fairtrade certification ensures that producers in developing countries receive a fair price for their goods, along with improved working conditions and community investment. Fairtrade products include coffee, tea, chocolate, bananas, and sugar. Buying Fairtrade supports sustainable livelihoods in poorer communities.

Primary processing is the first stage of turning raw food into something usable. Examples include: milling wheat into flour (cleaning, grinding, sieving), and heat-treating milk.

Milk undergoes different levels of heat treatment: pasteurised (heated to 72°C for 15 seconds — kills most harmful bacteria, short shelf life), UHT (ultra-high temperature, 135°C for 1–4 seconds — long shelf life, can be stored at room temperature), sterilised (heated above 100°C for longer — very long shelf life but altered flavour), and micro-filtered (passed through fine filters to remove bacteria — fresher taste than UHT).

Secondary processing turns primary-processed ingredients into finished products. Examples: flour → bread, pasta, cakes; milk → cheese, yoghurt, butter; fruit → jams, juices; meat → sausages, pies. This adds value and extends shelf life.

Processing can cause vitamin loss. Heat destroys vitamins B and C. Drying and milling remove nutrients from the outer layers of grains. This is why some products are fortified — nutrients are added back in.

Fortification is the addition of nutrients to food to improve its nutritional value. UK law requires white flour to be fortified with thiamin (vitamin B1), niacin (vitamin B3), calcium, and iron. Many breakfast cereals are fortified with folic acid (to help prevent neural tube defects) and iron. Margarine and spreads must contain added vitamins A and D. Some spreads are enriched with plant stanols/sterols to help lower cholesterol.

Food additives are substances added to food during processing. There are four main types:

Colourings — make food look more appealing (e.g. adding colour to sweets or soft drinks). Some artificial colourings have been linked to hyperactivity in children. Flavourings — enhance or add taste (e.g. vanilla flavouring in ice cream). Can be natural or artificial. Preservatives — extend shelf life by slowing bacterial growth or oxidation (e.g. salt, sugar, vinegar, sulphites). Emulsifiers and stabilisers — prevent mixtures from separating and maintain texture (e.g. lecithin in chocolate, xanthan gum in sauces).

Additives have pros (longer shelf life, improved safety, consistent quality, lower cost) and cons (some may cause allergic reactions, concerns about artificial ingredients, may mask poor-quality food). All approved additives in the UK are given an E-number and must be listed on food labels.

Key Fact

UK law requires white flour to be fortified with thiamin, niacin, calcium, and iron because milling removes nutrient-rich outer layers of the grain. Margarine must contain vitamins A and D. Cereals are often fortified with folic acid and iron. Fortification helps prevent nutritional deficiencies in the population.

Key Fact

The four types of food additive are: colourings (linked to hyperactivity), flavourings (natural or artificial), preservatives (extend shelf life, e.g. salt, sulphites), and emulsifiers/stabilisers (prevent separation, e.g. lecithin). All must have E-numbers and be listed on labels.
before.exam_tip_html: In AQA Food Preparation and Nutrition, questions about food provenance often ask you to evaluate or discuss. This means you must give both sides — advantages and disadvantages. For example, if asked about GM foods, write about higher yields and pest resistance (advantages) and long-term health concerns and ethical objections (disadvantages). Always use specific examples rather than vague statements: “golden rice has been genetically modified to contain beta-carotene to address vitamin A deficiency” is much stronger than “GM food can be healthier.” For fortification, learn the specific nutrients required by UK law.

knowledge_checks.q: What temperature is milk heated to during pasteurisation?
Which of these is an example of secondary processing?
What does the Fairtrade certification ensure?
options: Producers in developing countries receive a fair price and better working conditions
Food has been produced using organic farming methods
Food has been sourced locally within the UK

knowledge_checks.q: Which nutrients must be added to margarine and spreads by UK law?
What is the main environmental concern with high food miles?
options: Food loses its flavour during transport
Increased transport emissions contribute to a larger carbon footprint
Local farmers cannot compete with cheaper imports
Packaging waste increases during long-distance transport

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'food miles'.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for: The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is consumed/sold (1).

Accept: How far food has to travel from farm to plate.

practice_questions.text: State two nutrients that UK law requires white flour to be fortified with.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each correct nutrient, up to 2 marks.
• Thiamin / vitamin B1 (1)
• Niacin / vitamin B3 (1)
• Calcium (1)
• Iron (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between primary processing and secondary processing, giving one example of each.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each valid point, up to 4 marks.
• Primary processing: converting raw food into a usable form (1)
• Example: milling wheat into flour / pasteurising milk (1)
• Secondary processing: turning primary-processed ingredients into finished products (1)
• Example: flour into bread / milk into cheese / fruit into jam (1)

practice_questions.text: Describe two advantages and two disadvantages of organic farming.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each valid advantage/disadvantage, up to 4 marks.
Advantages:
• No synthetic pesticides/fertilisers — fewer chemical residues (1)
• Better for biodiversity/wildlife (1)
• Higher animal welfare standards (1)
• Better for soil health / crop rotation (1)
Disadvantages:
• Lower crop yields (1)
• Higher prices for consumers (1)
• More labour-intensive (1)
• More land needed to produce the same amount (1)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of food additives in processed food products.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (award marks across Level 1–3):
Top band (5-6): Detailed evaluation with balanced argument.
• Preservatives extend shelf life, reducing food waste
• Emulsifiers improve texture and consistency
• Colourings and flavourings make food more appealing
• Concerns: artificial colourings linked to hyperactivity in children
• May mask poor-quality ingredients
• Some people have allergies/intolerances to specific additives
• Balanced conclusion weighing benefits against concerns
Mid band (3-4): Sound evaluation with some balance.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points with limited evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the challenges to global food security and suggest ways in which food production could become more sustainable.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (award marks across Level 1–3):
Top band (5-6): Detailed discussion with well-developed suggestions.
• Growing population (9.7 billion by 2050) increases demand
• Climate change causes droughts, flooding, unpredictable seasons
• Urbanisation reduces agricultural land
• Solutions: reducing food waste at all stages of supply chain
• Sustainable farming practices (crop rotation, reduced pesticides)
• GM crops for drought resistance / higher yields
• Fairtrade to support producers in developing countries
• Buying local/seasonal to reduce food miles
Mid band (3-4): Sound discussion with some solutions.
Lower band (1-2): Basic understanding with limited suggestions.

before.exam_tip_html: When the AQA exam asks you to describe a cuisine, use the five-point framework: distinctive ingredients, cooking methods, equipment, eating patterns, and presentation. Structure your answer around these headings to cover all the marks. For sensory evaluation questions, always explain why controlled conditions matter — for example, “samples are coded with random numbers to prevent taster bias” is a stronger answer than “samples are labelled.” If asked to choose a sensory test for a scenario, name the test, explain how it works, and say why it is appropriate.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'cuisine'.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for: A style of cooking characteristic of a particular country, region, or culture (1).

Accept: A type of cooking from a specific country/area defined by its ingredients and methods.

practice_questions.text: Name two controlled conditions that should be used when carrying out a sensory test.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each valid condition, up to 2 marks.
• Quiet room / individual booths / no distractions (1)
• Samples same size/temperature/in identical containers (1)
• Samples coded with random numbers (1)
• Palate cleansers (water/crackers) between samples (1)
• White/neutral lighting (1)
• Clear written instructions for tasters (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how a triangle test works and when it would be used.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each valid point, up to 4 marks.
• Tasters are given three samples (1)
• Two are the same / one is different (1)
• Tasters must identify the odd one out (1)
• Used to find out if people can detect a difference between products (1)
• Useful when a recipe or ingredient has been changed (1)
• It is a discrimination test (1)

practice_questions.text: Describe three distinctive features of Italian cuisine. Include reference to ingredients, cooking methods, and eating patterns.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each valid point linked to the correct area, up to 4 marks.
Ingredients:
• Olive oil, tomatoes, garlic, basil, Parmesan, pasta, mozzarella (1)
Cooking methods:
• Boiling (pasta), sautéing (soffritto), grilling, roasting, baking (1)
• Emphasis on simplicity and quality of ingredients (1)
Eating patterns:
• Multi-course structure: antipasto, primo, secondo, dolce (1)
• Social occasions / meals eaten slowly with family (1)
Presentation:
• Simple, colourful, rustic / fresh herbs and olive oil as garnish (1)

practice_questions.text: Compare British and Indian cuisines. In your answer, refer to distinctive ingredients, cooking methods, and eating patterns.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (award marks across Level 1–3):
Top band (5-6): Detailed comparison across multiple areas.
• British: beef, lamb, root vegetables, dairy, wheat flour / Indian: spices (cumin, turmeric, chilli), rice, lentils, ghee, yoghurt
• British: roasting, baking, boiling, stewing / Indian: tempering spices, tandoor grilling, slow-cooking curries, deep frying
• British: three meals a day, individual plates / Indian: shared dishes, thali format, eating with the right hand
• British: simple, generous presentation / Indian: vibrant, colourful due to spices
Mid band (3-4): Sound comparison with some detail.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comparison with limited detail.

practice_questions.text: A food company wants to find out whether consumers prefer their original recipe or a new reduced-sugar version. Suggest a suitable sensory test, explain how it should be set up, and describe how the results should be recorded and analysed.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (award marks across Level 1–3):
Top band (5-6): Detailed, well-structured response.
• Paired preference test or hedonic test would be suitable
• Paired preference: give tasters both samples, ask which they prefer
• Hedonic: give both samples with a rating scale (e.g. 1–9)
• Controlled conditions: identical containers, same temperature, random 3-digit codes, palate cleansers, quiet room/booths
• Record on standardised score sheets
• Present as tally chart / bar chart / percentage of preferences
• Analyse: which product is preferred overall / by how much
Mid band (3-4): Sound answer with some setup detail.
Lower band (1-2): Basic answer naming a test only.
